paragraphs.title: The Crisis in Jerusalem and Hezekiah’s Appeal to Isaiah

answers: He rent his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth
easy.explanation: Hezekiah rent his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth.
easy.q: What did Hezekiah do when he heard Rabshakeh’s words?

easy.explanation: He went into the house of the Lord.
easy.q: Where did Hezekiah go after covering himself with sackcloth?

easy.explanation: They were sent unto Isaiah the prophet.
easy.q: To whom did Hezekiah send Eliakim, Shebna, and the elders of the priests?

answers: Assyria had threatened Jerusalem and blasphemed the living God
There was no harvest in Jerusalem
The king had gone into captivity
medium.explanation: The crisis involved Assyrian threats and blasphemy against God.
medium.q: Why did Hezekiah describe the situation as a day of trouble, rebuke, and blasphemy?

answers: Lift up his prayer for the remnant
medium.explanation: They asked Isaiah to pray for the remnant that was left.
medium.q: What did Hezekiah’s messengers ask Isaiah to do?

answers: Many children had been born in Jerusalem
The people were ready to go to war
The situation had reached a desperate crisis
medium.explanation: The image describes a critical situation with no strength to deliver.
medium.q: What does the image of children coming to the birth without strength to bring forth communicate?

answers: He sought spiritual help and prayer while facing the threat
He wanted to hide in the Temple
challenge.explanation: His actions show a turn toward God in prayer and through the prophet.
challenge.q: What can be learned from Hezekiah’s going into the house of the Lord before sending for Isaiah?

answers: Hezekiah should not be afraid of the Assyrian servants’ words
Judah had to make a covenant with Tirhakah
challenge.explanation: Isaiah told them, “Be not afraid” of the words they had heard.
challenge.q: What was the main message of Isaiah’s first reply?

answers: Sennacherib’s defeat, Hezekiah’s prayer, and the sending of messengers
The messengers were sent, Sennacherib was defeated, and Hezekiah rent his clothes
Assyrian threats, Hezekiah’s mourning, an appeal to Isaiah, and reassurance
challenge.explanation: This is the order of events in verses 1–7.
challenge.q: Which sequence correctly describes the events in this passage?

easy.explanation: He found Sennacherib warring against Libnah.
easy.q: Where did Rabshakeh find the king of Assyria?

easy.explanation: He heard that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia had come forth to make war.
easy.q: Whom did Sennacherib hear was coming to make war against him?

easy.explanation: He sent messengers to Hezekiah with threatening words.
easy.q: What did Sennacherib send to Hezekiah?

answers: That God could not deliver Jerusalem
medium.explanation: The message urged Hezekiah not to trust God to save Jerusalem.
medium.q: What did the Assyrian message try to make Hezekiah believe?

answers: To claim that Jerusalem also could not be delivered
To ask other kingdoms for help
medium.explanation: He used Assyria’s past conquests to intimidate Hezekiah.
medium.q: Why did Sennacherib mention the conquests of the kings of Assyria?

medium.explanation: In context, it means destroyed or laid waste.
medium.q: In the phrase “which my fathers have destroyed,” what does “destroyed” mean?

answers: The news caused Sennacherib to stop threatening Jerusalem
The news led Sennacherib to send another threatening message
The news caused Hezekiah to go out to battle
challenge.explanation: After hearing about Tirhakah, Sennacherib sent messengers to Hezekiah.
challenge.q: What was the connection between hearing about Tirhakah and sending messengers to Hezekiah?

answers: Jerusalem would be saved by its walls
The kings of Assyria were weaker than the nations
Hezekiah should not trust in God to deliver Jerusalem from Assyria
challenge.explanation: The message directly attacked Hezekiah’s confidence in God.
challenge.q: Which statement reflects the main point of the Assyrian mockery?

answers: Sennacherib was warring at Libnah and listed earlier conquests
challenge.explanation: Sennacherib’s military campaign and conquests demonstrated real power.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that the threat was more than merely verbal?

easy.explanation: He received the letter, read it, and spread it before the Lord.
easy.q: What did Hezekiah do with the letter he received from the messengers?

answers: Before the Lord in the house of the Lord
easy.explanation: He went into the house of the Lord and spread it before Him.
easy.q: Where did Hezekiah spread the letter?

answers: That all nations would serve Sennacherib
That the Lord would save Jerusalem and be known by all kingdoms
easy.explanation: He asked God to save Jerusalem so all kingdoms would know that He alone is Lord.
easy.q: What did Hezekiah ask at the end of his prayer?

answers: As the God alone of all the kingdoms of the earth, who made heaven and earth
medium.explanation: He declared that God alone rules all kingdoms and made heaven and earth.
medium.q: How did Hezekiah describe the God of Israel at the beginning of his prayer?

answers: To distinguish powerless idols from the living God
medium.explanation: He contrasted idols of wood and stone with the true God.
medium.q: Why did Hezekiah say that the gods of the nations were the work of men’s hands?

answers: A request for God to punish Hezekiah
A request for God to listen and see the reproach against Him
A request for the people to leave Jerusalem
medium.explanation: He asked God to hear and see Sennacherib’s words against Him.
medium.q: What does the request “Incline thine ear, O Lord, and hear” mean?

answers: He acknowledges Assyria’s power while trusting in the Lord’s supremacy
He wants to worship the gods of Assyria
He is deciding whether to move to Nineveh
challenge.explanation: He recognizes Assyria’s victories but affirms that the Lord alone is God.
challenge.q: What is the central tension in Hezekiah’s prayer?

answers: To show that the Lord alone is God
challenge.explanation: He wanted the salvation of Jerusalem to reveal God’s unique lordship.
challenge.q: Why is the deliverance Hezekiah requests connected with the knowledge of all the kingdoms of the earth?

answers: He mentions that God made heaven and earth
He asks God to hear the words of Sennacherib, who reproached the living God
He lists the number of Assyrian cities
challenge.explanation: He specifically asks God to hear Sennacherib’s reproach against Him.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that Hezekiah was concerned not only about danger but also about blasphemy?

paragraphs.title: God’s Answer and the Condemnation of Sennacherib’s Pride

easy.explanation: Isaiah sent the Lord’s word to Hezekiah.
easy.q: Who delivered the Lord’s answer to Hezekiah?

easy.explanation: The daughter of Zion is said to despise him and laugh him to scorn.
easy.q: How is Jerusalem’s attitude toward Sennacherib described?

answers: Coming up to the mountains and cutting down the cedars
easy.explanation: He boasted of reaching the mountains and cutting down their tall cedars.
easy.q: What did Sennacherib boast about doing?

answers: Because of his rage and pride against the Lord
medium.explanation: The Lord cited Sennacherib’s rage and tumult against Him.
medium.q: Why did the Lord say Sennacherib would be turned back to his own land?

answers: A branch growing in a field
A hook in the nose and a bridle in the lips
A shield protecting the city walls
medium.explanation: The Lord says He will put a hook in his nose and a bridle in his lips.
medium.q: What image describes the Lord’s control over Sennacherib?

answers: A high place or lofty height
medium.explanation: It refers to something elevated or above.
medium.q: In the phrase “thou hast lifted up thine eyes on high,” what does “on high” refer to?

answers: Sennacherib’s actions had no meaning, and the Lord ignored him
Sennacherib acted within what God had ordained, yet was judged for his pride and blasphemy
challenge.explanation: God had appointed the events, but Sennacherib was still condemned for his arrogant conduct.
challenge.q: How does the Lord’s answer combine Sennacherib’s responsibility with God’s control of history?

answers: The two kings possess equal power
Sennacherib, despite his strength, is subject to the Lord’s control
challenge.explanation: The image presents Sennacherib as one whom the Lord can control and turn back.
challenge.q: What does the image of the hook and bridle teach about the balance of power?

answers: Sennacherib boasts of his power, while the Lord declares that He can turn him back
Sennacherib asks for peace, while the Lord refuses
Sennacherib speaks of Jerusalem, while the Lord speaks only of Egypt
challenge.explanation: Human pride is set against the Lord’s authority over Sennacherib.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears between Sennacherib’s words and the Lord’s answer?

paragraphs.title: The Promise of Restoration and Protection

answers: Sow, reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit
easy.explanation: In the third year they would sow, reap, and plant vineyards.
easy.q: What would the people of Judah be able to do in the third year?

answers: Take root downward and bear fruit upward
easy.explanation: The remnant would take root downward and bear fruit upward.
easy.q: What would the remnant of the house of Judah do?

easy.explanation: He would not come into the city, shoot an arrow, or cast a bank against it.
easy.q: What was Sennacherib promised he would not do to Jerusalem?

answers: First vineyards, then famine, and finally war
First what grows of itself, then what springs from the same, and finally sowing and reaping
First harvest, then captivity, and finally planting
medium.explanation: The passage describes the first year’s growth, the second year’s growth, and full cultivation in the third.
medium.q: What is the order of agricultural recovery described in the passage?

medium.explanation: It refers to growth that comes naturally from what was previously sown.
medium.q: In the phrase “Ye shall eat this year such as groweth of itself,” what does “groweth of itself” mean?

answers: For the sake of the kings of Assyria
For His own sake and for His servant David’s sake
medium.explanation: The Lord promised to save the city for His own sake and David’s sake.
medium.q: For whose sake did the Lord say He would defend Jerusalem?

answers: Protection allows the remnant to remain in the land and continue life there
Restoration requires the people to move to Assyria
challenge.explanation: Deliverance from Assyria allows the remnant to survive, grow, and cultivate the land.
challenge.q: How are agricultural restoration and protection of Jerusalem connected?

answers: The remnant will remain hidden without a future
The remnant will become established in the land and produce new life
challenge.explanation: The image expresses stability, growth, and continuing life.
challenge.q: What does the image “take root downward, and bear fruit upward” mean?

answers: The people will eat what grows of itself
Sennacherib will neither shoot an arrow, come with shields, nor cast a bank against the city
challenge.explanation: Several forms of attack are specifically ruled out.
challenge.q: Which detail emphasizes that Jerusalem’s protection will be complete rather than partial?

paragraphs.title: The Defeat of the Assyrian Camp and Sennacherib’s End

easy.explanation: The angel of the Lord went forth and smote the Assyrian camp.
easy.q: Who smote the camp of the Assyrians?

answers: A hundred and fourscore and five thousand
easy.explanation: The KJV states that 185,000 were smitten.
easy.q: How many Assyrian soldiers were smitten?

easy.explanation: Esarhaddon, Sennacherib’s son, reigned in his stead.

medium.explanation: When they arose in the morning, they were all dead corpses.
medium.q: What was found in the Assyrian camp in the morning?

medium.explanation: He departed and went and returned to Nineveh.
medium.q: Where did Sennacherib go after the defeat?

answers: Worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god
medium.explanation: He was worshipping in the house of Nisroch when his sons smote him.
medium.q: What was Sennacherib doing when his sons killed him?

answers: Sennacherib withdrew after his camp was smitten
Hezekiah went out to fight him
challenge.explanation: The defeat of the Assyrian camp led Sennacherib to return to Nineveh.
challenge.q: How was the promise that Sennacherib would not enter Jerusalem fulfilled?

answers: The man who boasted of his power was humbled, withdrew, and was killed
challenge.explanation: His downfall directly contrasts with his earlier boasting.
challenge.q: What connection exists between Sennacherib’s end and the chapter’s theme of his pride?

answers: Sennacherib conquered Jerusalem, returned to Nineveh, and appointed Rabshakeh
The angel smote the camp, Sennacherib returned to Nineveh, his sons killed him, and Esarhaddon reigned
Tirhakah defeated the camp, Sennacherib surrendered to Hezekiah, and Esarhaddon fled
challenge.explanation: That is the sequence described in verses 36–38.
challenge.q: Which sequence correctly summarizes the end of the chapter?
